articles.title: ADA Compliant Ecommerce Checkout: WCAG Requirements for Form Labels, Error Handling, and Payment Widgets
articles.excerpt: Last spring I ran an accessibility audit for a Shopify store doing about $140,000 a year in revenue. The owner was convinced his site was fine because he had passed a free overlay widget scan. When I…
articles.body: Last spring I ran an accessibility audit for a Shopify store doing about $140,000 a year in revenue. The owner was convinced his site was fine because he had passed a free overlay widget scan. When I tested the checkout with a screen reader, the payment step announced only "edit text" seven times in a row. A blind customer literally could not tell which field was asking for a card number and which was asking for a ZIP code. He had been unknowingly turning away paying customers for months. Why Checkout Accessibility Matters More Than Any Other Page Your product pages get the traffic, but your checkout is where money changes hands. It is also where accessibility failures hurt most, because the user has already decided to buy and then hits a wall.
articles.author: Veduis

articles.title: Where do the ideas from your agent sessions go?
articles.excerpt: A long session with a coding agent produces more than code. A bug you noticed on the way. An idea for a feature. A "we should also..." that the agent agreed to. Then the session scrolls on, gets compa…
articles.body: A long session with a coding agent produces more than code. A bug you noticed on the way. An idea for a feature. A "we should also..." that the agent agreed to. Then the session scrolls on, gets compacted or closed, and the idea is gone. "Later" never comes, because nothing remembers it. I have lost enough of those to try several places for them. None is perfect, and I want to know what you use, so this is a comparison with a question at the end, not a recommendation. Scrolling back The default. It works until the context is compacted or the terminal closes, which with agents is a few hours at most. I count it here because most people I ask are still on it. A notes file in the repo A NOTES.md , a CLAUDE.md , or the agent's own memory.

articles.title: Your Lead Scoring Prompt Doesn't Need the Whole Row
articles.excerpt: Your token bill gets uncomfortable, and the qualification agent is still reading featureId. Somewhere, a hexadecimal identifier has acquired a consulting budget. Lab note 004: we wanted to know which…
articles.body: Your token bill gets uncomfortable, and the qualification agent is still reading featureId . Somewhere, a hexadecimal identifier has acquired a consulting budget. Lab note 004: we wanted to know which fields a lead qualification prompt actually needs when the listing schema exposes 24 fields. The catch comes early: inspecting a schema can justify a smaller context contract. It can't establish a token-savings percentage or an improvement in scoring accuracy. Those need measurements on your records and your qualification task. What does the scorer need to decide? Suppose you're building a queue of coffee shops in Austin for email outreach. The agent needs to assess category fit, apparent location, public reputation, and whether there's evidence of an email contact.

articles.title: Abliteration.ai for Security Teams: Refusal Removal, Policy Gateways, and AI Cyber Defense
articles.excerpt: A refusal from a frontier model is not a security control. It is a vendor decision about what that API will say. Abliteration.ai, at abliteration.ai, sells the opposite default: hosted models with ref…
articles.body: A refusal from a frontier model is not a security control. It is a vendor decision about what that API will say. Abliteration.ai, at abliteration.ai , sells the opposite default: hosted models with refusal behavior stripped back, plus an optional policy gateway where the customer decides what to allow, block, rewrite, redact, or escalate. Security teams are already arguing about it on Reddit, and a September 2026 TechCrunch test showed the hosted model answering requests that ordinary assistants refuse. That combination is why the product matters for AI cybersecurity defense. It is also why treating it as a how-to kit is the wrong read. The useful question is narrower.

articles.title: From vibe coding to governed development
articles.excerpt: In 1957, John Backus and his team at IBM presented a paper called The FORTRAN Automatic Coding System. The promise was in the name: you would describe the computation, and the machine would do the pro…
articles.body: In 1957, John Backus and his team at IBM presented a paper called The FORTRAN Automatic Coding System . The promise was in the name: you would describe the computation, and the machine would do the programming. It didn't end programming. It created far more of it — because the people writing FORTRAN no longer had to think in registers. Every step up the ladder has looked like that. Machine code gave way to assembly, assembly to high-level languages. Each step let people write less about how and more about what . And each step moved the source of truth up a level: once compilers could be trusted, nobody maintained the assembly. They maintained the source. Coding agents are the next step. What you hand an agent is, at bottom, a requirement: what the system should do.

articles.title: Agentic Vulnerability Discovery: Exploit Agents, Guardrails, and PoC Validation
articles.excerpt: Vulnerability research agents sit at the opposite end of the security spectrum from defensive tools. Instead of scanning code for bugs, they hunt for exploitable weaknesses, generate proof-of-concept…
articles.body: Vulnerability research agents sit at the opposite end of the security spectrum from defensive tools. Instead of scanning code for bugs, they hunt for exploitable weaknesses, generate proof-of-concept attacks, and prioritize threats based on real-world access patterns. Spencer McIntyre, Director of Exploit Development at VulnCheck, runs these agents in production and reports a consistent problem: most AI-generated exploits fail when pointed at actual targets. The gap between a working demo and a reliable exploit exposes the plumbing challenges unique to offensive security agents. These systems must balance capability with safety, validate outputs against live infrastructure, and hand off findings to human researchers without creating false confidence or wasted effort.

articles.title: RS-25 Engine Tests at NASA Stennis
articles.excerpt: Teams at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21, 2026. The hot fire test lasted for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the sam…
articles.body: NASA/Danny Nowlin Teams at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21, 2026. The hot fire test lasted for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, with a 111% power level. For each Artemis mission, four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket. Prior to use, all RS-25 engines are proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis. While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime engine contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability.

articles.body: Tim McCollum captured a stunning view of Orionid meteors in the early hours of Oct. 21. (Image credit: Tim McCollum) Astrophotographer Tim McCollum captured a spectacular view of Orionid meteors sharing the night sky with a host of deep sky wonders on Oct. 21, as the annual shooting star display ramped up to peak activity. Comet 1P/Halley may be over 3 billion miles (4.8 kilometers) from Earth , but that didn't stop it from putting on a breathtaking display earlier this week, as particles cast off by the ancient wanderer carved a fiery path through the autumn sky. McCollum was able to capture a trio of vivid Orionid meteors as they streaked through the night sky above the city of Toccoa, Georgia, between 3-4 a.m. on Oct. 21.

articles.title: Never finishing the fight: Where did Xbox go wrong with Halo?
articles.excerpt: After a failed soft reboot and a remake of the original, the Halo universe is facing yet another major creative shift. But has Xbox learned any lessons this time?
articles.body: Halo: Campaign Evolved was Xbox’s second attempt at refreshing the 2001 sci-fi FPS classic, and it is perfectly fine. A cromulent remake, if ever there was one, but it’s hardly a franchise-saver, especially as Xbox looks to rethink its studio structure and approach to renowned IPs like Halo or Gears of War . Halo hasn’t been the same since original developer Bungie — now owned by Sony and working on Destiny and Marathon — departed, leaving 343 Industries (now Halo Studios) to guide the franchise. Neither Halo 4 nor 5 meaningfully evolved the gameplay formula or overarching narrative. Halo Infinite found more success by reheating what “old Halo felt like” and sticking it into a half-baked open world, but it still felt far from the series’ glory days.
